title: The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 and burned for four days, destroying roughly 80%
description:
The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 and burned for four days, destroying roughly 80% of the walled city. It took four of the City's seven gates along with St Paul's Cathedral.

burned down in four days. The official death toll was six.

The Monument to the fire still carries the line: "Merciless to the wealth and estates of the citizens, it was harmless to their lives." The six recorded dead include a maid who could not escape the bakery where the fire started, and three bodies found mummified by heat inside St Paul's Cathedral.

Historians disagree on whether six is real. Adrian Tinniswood puts the toll in single figures; Neil Hanson argues it was several hundred, or quite possibly several thousand. Hanson's case rests on melted glass and iron found in the ruins: evidence the fire burned hotter than a modern crematorium, hot enough to leave no remains at all.

One death the toll does include is Robert Hubert, a French watchmaker who confessed to starting the fire and was hanged for it at Tyburn. He had changed his story once already, claiming Westminster before learning the fire never reached there, and a ship's captain later testified Hubert did not land in England until two days after it started.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hubert: confirms Robert Hubert, a French watchmaker, falsely confessed to starting the Great Fire; that he first claimed Westminster and changed his story once told the fire never reached there; that he claimed to throw a fire grenade through the Farriner bakery's open window despite the bakery having no window and Hubert being judged too crippled to throw anything; that a captain of the Maid of Stockholm later testified he had landed Hubert in England two days after the fire started; and that Hubert was hanged at Tyburn on 27 October 1666, his body torn apart by a crowd before it could be handed over for dissection.
- https://londonist.com/2016/08/is-it-true-that-only-six-people-died-in-the-great-fire: confirms the fire destroyed roughly four-fifths of London including about 13,200 houses, four of the City's seven gates and St Paul's Cathedral; the Monument's inscription ("Merciless to the wealth and estates of the citizens, it was harmless to their lives"); the identities described for several of the six officially recorded dead, including a maid at the Farriner bakery and three bodies mummified by heat inside St Paul's Cathedral; and the historians' disagreement over the true toll, with Adrian Tinniswood putting it "in single figures" and Neil Hanson arguing for "several hundred, or quite possibly several thousand", citing melted glass and iron found in the ruins as evidence the fire burned hotter than a modern crematorium.
